```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(targets)
library(ggplot2)
tar_source("R")
tar_load(c(velib, summary, pca, components_90, kmeans_fits, ward, mixtures, gap, stability,
           validity, benchmark, neighbours, spatial, moran, bonus))

ink <- "#1B1B19"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      text = element_text(colour = ink), axis.text = element_text(colour = ink),
      panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 0.3), legend.position = "bottom",
      # White, so the image can be blended onto whichever paper the reader chose.
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      strip.text = element_text(colour = ink, hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
)
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f%%"), 100 * x)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
X <- velib$profiles
time <- velib$time
four <- kmeans_fits[[3]]
groups <- describe_clusters(velib, summary, four$cluster)
labels <- vapply(groups, function(g) g$label, character(1))
at <- function(table, k, column) table[[column]][table$k == k]
day_axis <- scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(12, 156, 24), labels = DAYS, expand = c(0, 0))
day_lines <- geom_vline(xintercept = seq(24, 144, 24), linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey75")
shapes <- c(15, 6, 17, 0)
```

## Summary

This is a rework of an exam I wrote in 2021. The data are one week of hourly readings from
the `r nrow(X)` stations of Vélib, the Paris bike-sharing system. The question is whether
stations fall into types, and what the types mean.

- **Two patterns carry `r pct(sum(pca$explained[1:2]))` of the variation between stations.**
  The first (`r pct(pca$explained[1])`) is how full a station is all week. The second
  (`r pct(pca$explained[2])`) is whether it fills or empties during the working day.
- **Clusters built from timetables alone are neighbourhoods.** With four clusters,
  `r pct(at(spatial, 4, "observed"))` of a station's six nearest neighbours share its cluster.
  Random labels would give `r pct(at(spatial, 4, "expected"))`. The clustering was never given
  a coordinate.
- **The empty cluster is the hills.** `r pct(bonus$emptiest_cluster_share)` of the
  `r bonus$n` uphill "bonus" stations fall in one cluster, the one that is nearly always
  empty. They hold bikes in `r pct(bonus$mean_fill_bonus)` of their docks, against
  `r pct(bonus$mean_fill_other)` elsewhere.
- **There is no natural number of clusters.** Silhouettes are low
  (at most `r num(max(validity$silhouette))`), the gap statistic never peaks, and three
  clustering methods agree only partly. The stations form a continuum. But cutting it into
  two, three or four is repeatable under resampling (adjusted Rand index
  `r num(at(validity, 4, "stability_ari"))` at four), and cutting it into five is not
  (`r num(at(validity, 5, "stability_ari"))`).
- **The 2021 version made three mistakes** that this one corrects: it clustered on a column
  that duplicated information, used a linkage that chases outliers, and chose the number of
  clusters by eye.

The [web page](../) lets you explore the map.

## Data

The dataset comes from Bouveyron, Côme and Jacques
([2015](https://doi.org/10.1214/15-AOAS861)), who collected it from the operator's open data
feed and distribute it with the R package `funFEM`. Each station reports its *loading*: the
share of its docks holding a bike, between 0 and 1, once an hour. Alongside are each
station's coordinates and a flag for "bonus" stations, which sit on high ground. The operator
rewarded riders for returning bikes there, because people ride down from them and do not
ride back up.

The recording starts on a Sunday at 11:00. Those first 13 hours are an incomplete day and
are dropped, leaving `r ncol(X)` hours from Monday 00:00 to Sunday 23:00. There are no
missing values.

```{r week}
#| fig-cap: "Average loading across all stations, hour by hour. The bikes are conserved, so the average barely moves: what changes over the day is where they are."
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(data.frame(hour = time$index - 0.5, loading = colMeans(X)), aes(hour, loading)) +
  day_lines + geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) + day_axis +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Docks holding a bike")
```

## What was wrong with the first version

| 2021 notebook | This version | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Appended each station's weekly mean to the data, then ran PCA, k-means and hierarchical clustering on all 169 columns | Clusters on the 168 hourly loadings only | The mean is a linear combination of the other columns. Adding it counts the overall level twice and changes every distance |
| Hierarchical clustering with complete linkage | Ward's method | Complete linkage merges on the single most distant pair, so a few odd stations decide the tree. Ward minimises within-cluster variance, the same criterion as k-means |
| Chose four clusters by looking at a curve of explained variance | Gap statistic, silhouette, bootstrap stability, and a no-cluster benchmark | "The elbow looks like four" is not evidence. It turns out four is defensible, but for a different reason |
| Described the map by eye | Permutation test of spatial coherence | The claim that clusters are neighbourhoods can be tested |
| Random starts without a seed | Seeded, cluster labels ordered by fill level | Results did not reproduce from run to run |

## Two components

```{r pca}
#| fig-cap: "Weight of each hour in the first two principal components."
#| fig-height: 3.2
loadings <- data.frame(hour = rep(time$index - 0.5, 2),
                       component = rep(c("1: fill level", "2: working day"), each = 168),
                       weight = c(pca$rotation[, 1], pca$rotation[, 2]))
ggplot(loadings, aes(hour, weight, linetype = component)) +
  day_lines + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.2) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  day_axis + labs(x = NULL, y = "Loading", linetype = NULL)
```

The analysis is on the covariance matrix: all 168 columns are on the same scale, so they are
centred but not standardised.

The first component has the same sign at every hour. A station's score on it correlates
`r num(cor(pca_scores(pca, X, 1)[, 1], summary$mean_fill), 3)` with its weekly mean: it is
the fill level. The second is positive from about nine to six on weekdays and negative at
night, with a weaker and later version of the same shape at the weekend. Stations with a
high score receive bikes during the working day; stations with a low score send them.

After that the components fall away quickly (`r pct(pca$explained[3], 1)`,
`r pct(pca$explained[4], 1)`, ...). Reaching 90% of the variance takes `r components_90`
components, so two dimensions are a summary, not the whole story. Clustering is therefore
done on all 168 hours, not on the scores.

Both components are strongly organised in space, which already hints at what the clustering
will find. Moran's I, with each station's six nearest neighbours as its neighbourhood, is
`r num(moran[[1]]$observed)` for the first component and `r num(moran[[2]]$observed)` for the
second (0 means no spatial pattern; both p = `r num(moran[[1]]$p, 3)` by permutation).

## How many clusters?

```{r validity}
tab <- data.frame(
  K = validity$k,
  `Variance explained` = pct(validity$r2),
  Silhouette = num(validity$silhouette),
  `Silhouette, no clusters` = num(benchmark$silhouette),
  Gap = num(validity$gap),
  `Stability (ARI)` = num(validity$stability_ari),
  `Stability, no clusters` = num(benchmark$stability_ari),
  `Weakest cluster (Jaccard)` = num(validity$weakest_jaccard),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(tab, align = "r")
```

Four different questions are being asked here.

**Are the groups separated?** No. The average silhouette width is
`r num(max(validity$silhouette))` at best. Kaufman and Rousseeuw's rule of thumb reads 0.26
to 0.50 as weak structure that could be artificial, and 0.25 or below as none.

**Is there more clustering than in structureless data?** A little. The "no clusters" columns
come from a simulated dataset with the same covariance as the real one but drawn from a
single Gaussian: an ellipsoidal cloud with no groups in it. k-means will happily cut such a
cloud into pieces, and its silhouettes (`r num(at(benchmark, 4, "silhouette"))` at K = 4) are
not far below the real ones (`r num(at(validity, 4, "silhouette"))`).

**Does some K stand out?** No. The gap statistic rises all the way to K = 8, so the usual
rule picks the largest K offered (`r gap$chosen`). The mixture model's BIC does the same up
to K = `r mixtures$bic$k[which.max(mixtures$bic$bic)]`. Neither is a sign of
`r gap$chosen` real groups; it is what happens when a smooth distribution is approximated
by more and more pieces.

**Is the partition repeatable?** Up to four, yes. Stability is measured by drawing 100
bootstrap samples of stations, clustering each, assigning every station to its nearest new
centre and comparing with the original partition by the adjusted Rand index (1 is identical,
0 is chance).

```{r stability}
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap stability of the k-means partition. Bars: 10th to 90th percentile over 100 resamples. Dashed: simulated data with no clusters."
#| fig-height: 3.2
stab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(stability), function(i) {
  q <- quantile(stability[[i]]$ari, c(0.1, 0.9))
  data.frame(k = validity$k[i], mean = mean(stability[[i]]$ari), lo = q[1], hi = q[2])
}))
ggplot(stab, aes(k, mean)) +
  geom_line(data = benchmark, aes(k, stability_ari), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) + geom_point(shape = 15, size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = validity$k) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.4, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Number of clusters", y = "Adjusted Rand index")
```

At two, three and four clusters the partition comes back almost unchanged
(`r num(at(validity, 2, "stability_ari"))`, `r num(at(validity, 3, "stability_ari"))`,
`r num(at(validity, 4, "stability_ari"))`), far above the structureless benchmark. At five it
drops to `r num(at(validity, 5, "stability_ari"))`, and its least stable cluster overlaps
its bootstrap counterpart by only `r pct(at(validity, 5, "weakest_jaccard"))`.

So the honest description is this. The stations are a continuum with two strong directions
in it. There are no gaps to find. But the continuum is not round, and the first few cuts
through it fall in the same places every time. Four is the finest resolution that holds
still, and that is the reason to use it. It is a choice of resolution, not a count of
species.

### Do the methods agree?

```{r agreement}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  K = validity$k,
  `k-means vs Ward` = num(validity$ari_ward),
  `k-means vs Gaussian mixture` = num(validity$ari_mixture),
  `Mixture covariance model` = mixtures$bic$model[-1],
  check.names = FALSE
), align = "r")
```

Ward's method, which optimises the same criterion greedily, agrees fairly well with k-means
at four clusters (ARI `r num(at(validity, 4, "ari_ward"))`). A Gaussian mixture on the first
five principal components (`r pct(sum(pca$explained[1:5]))` of the variance) agrees much
less (`r num(at(validity, 4, "ari_mixture"))`). It is free to fit elongated, overlapping
components of different sizes, and with no gaps in the data to constrain it, it draws the
boundaries elsewhere. That disagreement is further evidence for a continuum: when groups are
real, methods find the same ones.

## The four clusters

```{r profiles}
#| fig-cap: "Mean loading of each cluster over the week."
#| fig-height: 5.2
centres <- do.call(rbind, lapply(groups, function(g) {
  data.frame(hour = time$index - 0.5, loading = g$centre,
             cluster = sprintf("%s (%d stations)", g$label, g$n))
}))
centres$cluster <- factor(centres$cluster, unique(centres$cluster))
ggplot(centres, aes(hour, loading)) + day_lines + geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~cluster, ncol = 1) + day_axis +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Docks holding a bike")
```

```{r describe}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Cluster = labels,
  Stations = vapply(groups, function(g) g$n, numeric(1)),
  `Mean loading` = pct(vapply(groups, function(g) g$mean_fill, numeric(1))),
  `Day minus night` = sprintf("%+.2f", vapply(groups, function(g) g$day_night, numeric(1))),
  `Bonus stations` = bonus$by_cluster$bonus,
  check.names = FALSE
), align = "lrrrr")
```

Cluster names are generated from two descriptors: the mean loading, and the weekday
difference between working hours (10:00 to 16:00) and the small hours (01:00 to 06:00).
Neither was used to form the clusters.

```{r scores}
#| fig-cap: "Stations on the first two principal components, marked by cluster. There are no gaps between the groups: the boundaries are cuts through a continuous cloud."
#| fig-height: 4.6
scores <- as.data.frame(pca_scores(pca, X, 2))
names(scores) <- c("pc1", "pc2")
scores$cluster <- factor(labels[four$cluster], labels)
ggplot(scores, aes(pc1, pc2, shape = cluster)) + geom_point(size = 1.1, stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = shapes) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Component 1: fill level", y = "Component 2: working day", shape = NULL) +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 2)))
```

## Are the clusters neighbourhoods?

```{r map}
#| fig-cap: "The stations, marked by cluster. Coordinates played no part in forming the clusters."
#| fig-height: 5
map <- data.frame(velib$stations[c("x", "y")], cluster = factor(labels[four$cluster], labels))
ggplot(map, aes(x, y, shape = cluster)) + geom_point(size = 1.1, stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = shapes) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "km east of centre", y = "km north of centre", shape = NULL) +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 2)))
```

The test is a join count. For every station, take its six nearest neighbours and count how
many share its cluster. Then shuffle the cluster labels over the stations 999 times and
count again. If where a station is had nothing to do with how it behaves, the observed share
would look like the shuffled ones.

```{r spatial}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  K = spatial$k,
  `Neighbours in same cluster` = pct(spatial$observed, 1),
  `Expected if random` = pct(spatial$expected, 1),
  `Highest of 999 shuffles` = pct(spatial$null_max, 1),
  z = num(spatial$z, 1),
  check.names = FALSE
), align = "r")
```

At every resolution the observed share is more than twice what chance gives and far beyond
anything the shuffles produced. A station's timetable is, to a large degree, a statement
about where it is.

This is not circular, but it is not mysterious either. Bikes move between nearby stations,
and nearby stations share the same land use and the same slope. The clustering recovers
geography because geography is what drives the timetable.

### The hills

The bonus flag gives an independent check on one cluster. It marks stations on high ground.

```{r bonus}
#| fig-cap: "Weekly mean loading of bonus (uphill) stations and all others."
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(data.frame(fill = summary$mean_fill,
                  kind = ifelse(velib$stations$bonus, "Bonus (uphill)", "Other")),
       aes(fill, kind)) +
  geom_boxplot(linewidth = 0.3, outlier.size = 0.6, width = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean share of docks holding a bike", y = NULL)
```

The `r bonus$n` bonus stations hold bikes in `r pct(bonus$mean_fill_bonus)` of their docks
on average, against `r pct(bonus$mean_fill_other)` for the rest. A randomly chosen bonus
station is emptier than a randomly chosen other station `r pct(bonus$prob_emptier)` of the
time. And `r bonus$by_cluster$bonus[4]` of the `r bonus$n`
(`r pct(bonus$emptiest_cluster_share)`) are in the "`r labels[4]`" cluster, which the
algorithm found without knowing which stations they were. That cluster is larger than the
hills, though: `r pct(1 - bonus$by_cluster$share[4])` of its stations are not bonus stations.
It also takes in much of the outer ring of the city.

## Limitations

- **One week.** Early September 2014, with whatever weather and events it had. Nothing here
  says the pattern holds in February. The system itself was replaced in 2018.
- **Loading is not demand.** A station at 0% tells you bikes were wanted and not how many.
  A full station hides people who wanted to return a bike and could not. The operator also
  moves bikes by truck, and that is in the data too.
- **Hours are treated as unordered columns.** Euclidean distance on 168 columns does not
  know that 08:00 and 09:00 are adjacent, so two stations with the same rush an hour apart
  look as different as two unrelated ones. The functional methods of the original paper
  address this; they are not reproduced here.
- **Names for clusters are a convenience.** "Fills by day" describes a cluster's average. The
  stations in it range continuously into their neighbours.
- **The geography is described, not modelled.** No land-use, altitude or transit data were
  joined. "Business core" and "residential" are readings of the map.

## Reproducing this

```sh
Rscript -e 'renv::restore()'
Rscript -e 'targets::tar_make()'    # data -> models -> validation -> JSON -> this report
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'
npm test                            # the page's arithmetic, checked against R
```

The page assigns stations to cluster centres and projects them onto the principal components
in JavaScript. The pipeline exports fixtures computed in R from the same JSON the page
loads, and a test requires the JavaScript to reproduce them.
